article.title: 2026 Los Angeles Midterms: How Grassroots Organizing Powered Progressive Wins
article.author: Sharon Kyle
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Before Dick Price and I started LA Progressive, I went to the county registrar to look up election returns for our congressional district. I think I was planning to write something for our Democratic club. What I remember clearly is how saddened I was by how few people had voted. Nearly two decades later, I sat down with Hans Johnson of the East Area Progressive Democrats to talk about a very different election. I was still taking in the news from Mississippi , where Scott Colom had become the first Black person elected to represent the state in the U.S. Senate since Reconstruction. Here in Los Angeles County , the latest count put turnout at 53.84 percent as of November 17, up from 43.65 percent in the 2022 midterm. The county had already counted more than 3.18 million ballots. I wanted to know what had changed here at home and what we could do with the opportunity voters had given us. Hans Johnson on Progressive L.A. Candidates (26:51) What it took to get voters to the polls Johnson called it a “bright blue wave of turnout.” He saw the No Kings protests as an early sign of how many people were ready to push back against the Trump administration. He also pointed to work closer to home that gets considerably less attention. Volunteers wrote postcards, neighbors met candidates, and voters got information from people they already knew and trusted. Johnson counted five victories in races his club had made priorities in November. Nithya Raman defeated incumbent Karen Bass for mayor, Marissa Roy won the city attorney’s race, Sara Hernandez won the 26th State Senate District, and Angela Gonzales-Torres unseated Rep. Jimmy Gomez in the 34th Congressional District. In the statewide race for superintendent of public instruction, Richard Barrera won after campaigning against what he called the “cage of austerity” in public education. Barri Worth Girvan’s City Council victory in the West Valley also prompted Johnson to reflect on the years of organizing it took to open up a council long dominated by men. I’m a member of the East Area Progressive Democrats, and when I make it to a meeting, I’m struck by how much people know about what’s happening in their own communities. I asked Hans how he keeps up. His answer was simple. He listens. Members bring reports on transit, public education and gun violence prevention. They ask questions and share articles so people can read up on an issue and decide whether to raise it with the officials who have the power to act. LAist included the club’s ballot guide in its roundup this fall. The meetings gave me a sense of how much work goes into earning the trust that makes people reach for a guide in the first place. What happens after the votes are counted I’d seen anti-gondola signs in my neighborhood, so I asked Hans what was behind them. The proposed aerial gondola would connect Union Station to Dodger Stadium, with a stop at Los Angeles State Historic Park near Chinatown. The project’s backers present it as a zero-emission way to get to the stadium. Johnson said the club opposes it because of its potential impact on public parkland and his concern about whether the public could end up paying for it. On December 2, the California State Park and Recreation Commission is scheduled to consider an amendment to the park’s general plan for the project. The election is over, and decisions about who gets to use public land and for what purpose are already on the calendar. The same question about what follows an election applies to the people we’ve just elected. In the county’s November 17 count, Gonzales-Torres was ahead of Gomez by more than 24 percentage points. Johnson remembered her high school teachers getting involved in the campaign and club volunteers helping to write thousands of postcards. He was especially moved to hear her talk about deported veterans as the daughter of one herself. She’ll be my representative, too. I want her to succeed, and I want us to pay attention to the rules and institutions that can keep even good candidates from delivering on the promises that got them elected. On November 18, Rep.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres voted against nominating Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker in a secret ballot of House Democrats. Jeffries won the nomination 251–11, with two Democrats casting no ballot. The full House will elect the speaker in January. Gonzales-Torres was one of eight incoming members who publicly confirmed voting against Jeffries. The other seven were Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Don Leonard of Ohio, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania. Three of the 11 votes against Jeffries were still publicly unconfirmed when Axios reported the tally. Texas Rep.-elect Frederick Haynes III signed the statement opposing Jeffries, but his spokesperson said he missed the vote. He was one of the two who did not cast a ballot. I’m still in wait-and-see mode about the progressive chops of the people we just elected. Gonzales-Torres was willing to break with most of her caucus on this vote. I’ll be watching how she votes on legislation and what she does when party leaders resist the policies she campaigned on. Johnson made a similar point about Sheriff Robert Luna, who had roughly 70 percent of the vote in his rematch with Alex Villanueva. Johnson welcomed the result and said the department still needs stronger civilian oversight and more transparency. Johnson said his club organized six No Kings rallies, primarily in Glendale. He wants those gatherings to continue. The people who came out to challenge Trump, he argued, can also keep the pressure on the people they helped elect. I’m still on a bit of a high from this election. I also remember walking out of the registrar’s office years ago wondering what it would take to get more of us involved. This November, hundreds of thousands more people in Los Angeles County voted than in the last midterm. I want us to bring some of that same energy to the places where decisions get made between elections. That’s where we’ll find out how much we changed.
